# Data and lineage

```{r}
#| include: false
source(here::here("chapters", "_setup.R"))
```

## Source

The data are one file, `licorice_gargle.csv`, emailed by the PI's fellow.
It is the public version of the trial data from the `medicaldata` R
package, with one row per patient. The codebook is
`notes/2026-10-16-codebook.md`. The file's date of receipt and its MD5
checksum are in `data/raw/README.md`. The raw file is never edited, and
`scripts/02_make_analysis_data.R` refuses to run if its bytes change
(D-019).

Cleaning (`clean_raw()`) checks every column against the codebook. An
unexpected code, an out-of-range or fractional score, or text in a numeric
column stops the pipeline and names the rows. The delivered file passed
every check. The file has no patient identifier, so each patient's
identifier is their row number in the raw file.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr '!has_data'
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat("*No data yet. Run `make results` once the raw file is in `data/raw/`.*\n")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_data
n_arm <- results$n_by_arm
miss <- results$missing
```

`r if (has_data) sprintf("The file has %d patients: %d randomized to sugar water and %d to licorice.", results$n_patients, n_arm[["Sugar water"]], n_arm[["Licorice"]]) else ""`
The codebook gives a higher enrollment count than the number of rows in the
file. Why some enrolled patients are absent is an open question for the
client (Chapter 1). If a randomized patient is missing, the analysis is
not fully intention to treat.

## Missing data

Any missing score is treated as missing, and each analysis uses the
patients observed at that assessment (complete case; D-010, D-015).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_data
#| tbl-cap: "Patients missing the sore-throat score at each assessment, by arm."
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Assessment = miss$assessment,
    `Sugar water` = sprintf("%d of %d", miss$missing_sugar, miss$n_sugar),
    Licorice = sprintf("%d of %d", miss$missing_licorice, miss$n_licorice),
    `Missing overall` = fmt_pct(miss$prop_missing, 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)
```

`r if (has_data) sprintf("Missing outcomes come entirely from %d patients (%d in each arm) who have no post-operative data at all; every other patient has all four scores.", results$no_postop_n, miss$missing_sugar[1]) else ""`
The intake notes anticipated this ("a couple pts no post-op data"), and
why those patients have no post-operative data is an open question in
Chapter 1.
`r if (has_data) sprintf("At most %s of patients are missing any one assessment.", fmt_pct(max(miss$prop_missing), 1)) else ""`
That is below the plan's five-percent trigger for revisiting the
missing-data approach (D-015), so the complete-case analyses stand.

### Best- and worst-case bounds for the primary outcome

The plan bounds the primary odds ratio by filling in every missing primary
outcome in the way most and least favourable to licorice (Chapter 3).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_data
#| tbl-cap: "Primary odds ratio (licorice against sugar water) with missing outcomes filled in."
b <- results$bounds
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Bound = b$bound,
    `Outcomes filled in` = b$n_filled,
    `Odds ratio (95% CI)` = fmt_or_cell(b$or, b$lower, b$upper),
    `p-value` = fmt_p(b$p_value),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)
```

`r if (has_data) sprintf("In the best case for licorice the odds ratio is %s; in the worst case it is %s. The complete-case estimate (Chapter 6) is %s.", fmt_or(results$bounds[1, ]), fmt_or(results$bounds[2, ]), fmt_or(results$primary)) else ""`
`r if (has_data) (if (all(results$bounds$upper < 1)) "Both bounds keep the confidence interval below one, so the missing outcomes cannot change the primary conclusion." else "At least one bound has a confidence interval that includes one, so the missing outcomes could change the primary conclusion.") else ""`
